newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Indian independence, triumph or tragedy for Britain?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Indian independence, triumph or tragedy for Britain?.

text.p: Working in the searing Indian heat with a stack of maps and a census, an obscure English barrister had just 36 days to partition British India into two separate and ultimately hostile states.

The borders that sprang from Cyril Radcliffe's pen plunged the subcontinent into violent upheaval, unleashing the greatest migration in human history and a frenzied bloodbath that left up to one million dead.

As India and Pakistan mark the 50th anniversary of their creation on August 15, 1947, historians and writers cannot agree whether Britain must bear the blame for the division and bloodshed or whether the colonial power did its best in a volatile and violence-prone region.

Writer Salman Rushdie, born to a Moslem family in Bombay two months before independence, asked: "Why on earth would anyone want to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of one of the century's great tragedies?"
Most experts agree that by the time Britain sent its last viceroy, Lord Louis Mountbatten, to India in March 1947 to sort out an eventual handover, a divided region had long since become inevitable.
Britain originally intended to lower the Union Jack in June 1948 but Mountbatten, seeing the chaos on the ground, moved the date forward.
The spotlight thus fell on Radcliffe, who had never been to the subcontinent before, had no special Indian expertise or even knowledge of cartography.

Yet he was given the impossible task of splitting 400 million people along religious lines based on the most recent population count -- mainly Hindu India was to receive 82.5 percent of the territory and Islamic Pakistan 17.5 percent.

But after centuries of coexistence, the interwoven Sikh, Moslem, and Hindu populations could not be separated by even the most creative of map-making, particularly in the scorched fields of the Punjab in the northwest and the lush paddies of Bengal in the east.
WARS AND VIOLENCE
Since 1947, the Indian subcontinent has suffered three wars, countless outbreaks of violence and an on-going cold war that still risks heating up.

Scholars continue to debate whether India needed to be partitioned into an Islamic and a largely Hindu state or if the 100 million Muslims could have been accommodated within a unified, federal nation.

By 1947 India had already begun to spin out of control with Moslem-Hindu and Moslem-Sikh violence and distrust spreading, beginning with communal riots in Calcutta in the summer of 1946, according to Anita Inder Singh, author of "Origins of the Partition of India".
Administrative disarray would sow the seeds of division.
"Britain had no choice but partition," said Lawrence James, author of "The Rise and Fall of the British Empire".

"The alternative was to face a massive collapse of civil order, possibly civil war, with no means of containing it. Pakistan had to be created because the alternative is too terrible to be contemplated," he said in an interview.

Moslem political leaders, headed by Mohammad Ali Jinnah and his All India Moslem League, grew increasingly insistent in their demands for an independent Moslem homeland free from what they saw as dominance by the Hindu majority. As a minority they saw little chance for success at the ballot box in a unified democracy.
But the Indian National Congress, led by Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, independent India's first prime minister, opposed compromise with the Moslems.
TRAPPED BETWEEN HOSTILE FACTIONS
At the end of World War Two, an exhausted Britain found itself trapped between these two increasingly hostile factions at the same time that its colonial administration was becoming ineffectual.

"The British left India because they lost control over crucial areas of the administration, and lacked the will and the financial or military ability to recover that control," said Patrick French, author of "Liberty or Death: India's Journey to Independence and Division", in an interview.
Britain's biggest mistake, according to many academics, was the belief that it could somehow impose order through a redrawing of the borders, that the different populations would sort themselves out.
But at independence and partition, the colonial army was suddenly paralysed. It, too, had to be divided between India and Pakistan, everything from guns down to typewriters.
A woefully-inadequate British force and the newly divided armies of Pakistan and India were powerless to police the new borders and stop the post-independence massacres.

But if Britain's hasty and clumsy retreat contributed to the upheaval it by no means caused it, scholars say. The hostile leaders of the Moslem League and the Congress ensured a peaceful solution would never be found.
"It was not a totalitarian state. Britain could not tell 400 million subjects to do something they did not want to do," said James.

Partition might have been avoided if a whole chain of events had not occurred -- if the British had developed a more concerted colonial policy; if the police had stamped out communal violence as soon as it broke out; and, most importantly, if the leaders of the rival political and religious factions had looked beyond their own jealousies and ambitions for power.

In the words of Salman Rushdie: "I would argue partition was an avoidable mistake, the result not of historical inevitability or the true will of the people but of political antagonisms -- between Gandhi and...Jinnah, between the Congress Party and the Moslem League."

But if India's geographic integrity had been preserved and the Moslems somehow accommodated within a secular, but predominantly Hindu country, the question inevitably becomes: Could it have survived? With such modern examples of Bosnia, Israel, Northern Ireland and Cyprus, many doubt the answer could ever have been yes.

"Even if unity had somehow been preserved, the forces of Asian religious nationalism and Moslem fundamentalism would have put enormous strains on any unified country," concluded Christopher Bayly, an Indian historian at Cambridge University. "One wonders whether it could have survived and the answer is probably not."
